title: Regularity and Weyl orbit of the half sum of positive roots
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $G$ be a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected, affine and of finite type with trivial smooth connected normal unipotent radical. Fix a split maximal torus $T$, a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$, and its finite reduced crystallographic root datum, character lattice $X=X^*(T)$, positive roots $\Phi^+$, simple roots $\Delta$ and coroots as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. In the rational span $E$ of the roots inside $X\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, put $\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$. Let $W=N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$ act by $(w\chi)(t)=\chi(n_w^{-1}tn_w)$. Then $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$ for every $\alpha\in\Delta$, and the only $w\in W$ satisfying $w\rho=\rho$ is $1$. There is a unique $w_0\in W$ with $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$; it satisfies $w_0^2=1$ and $w_0\rho=-\rho$, and $$w\rho=-\rho\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=w_0.$$ These are identities in the rational character space, so hold for groups in any characteristic. When $\Phi$ is empty, $E=0$, $W=\{1\}$ and $w_0=1$.

source.place: Appendix C.21--C.22 (p.613), Weyl chambers and the simply transitive Weyl action; Summary 21.41 and Definition 21.72 (p.447). Agent-formulated consequence: a simple reflection permutes the positive roots other than its simple root, hence s_alpha(rho)=rho-alpha, so rho is in the open dominant chamber, with trivial stabilizer.

proof.text: The Borel-pair node gives the finite reduced crystallographic root datum and its simple-root base $\Delta$, so every positive root is an integral nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. By [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization], the given quotient $W$ acts faithfully on $E$ and is exactly its root reflection group. In particular it is finite. These are the group and root system to which the chamber theorem will be applied; no faithfulness of a Lie algebra differential is asserted.

Fix $\alpha\in\Delta$. If $\beta\in\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha\}$, some coefficient of $\beta$ at a simple root other than $\alpha$ is positive: otherwise reducedness would give $\beta=\alpha$. In $s_\alpha\beta=\beta-\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ that coefficient is unchanged. As this is a root and all simple coefficients of a root have the same sign, it is positive. It cannot equal $\alpha$, since applying the involution $s_\alpha$ would give $\beta=-\alpha$. Thus $s_\alpha$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha\}$ and sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$.

source.place: C.21, p.612; elementary coefficient argument from the base and reflection definitions.

proof.text: Reindex the finite sum using the preceding permutation. Then $s_\alpha\rho=\rho-\alpha$. The reflection formula also gives $s_\alpha\rho=\rho-\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. Subtracting and using $\alpha\ne0$ in the rational vector space gives $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$. This calculation takes place in $X\otimes\mathbf Q$, where $2$ is invertible, regardless of the characteristic of $F$.

source.place: C.21, p.612; explicit half-sum calculation following the source of the item.

proof.text: Put $V=E\otimes_{\mathbf Q}\mathbf R$. In any real basis choose the usual dot product $(\ ,\ )_0$ and set $(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}(wx,wy)_0$. Reindexing proves $W$-invariance, and the identity summand makes this form positive definite. For a root $\alpha$, invariance and $s_\alpha\alpha=-\alpha$ give $(s_\alpha x,\alpha)=-(x,\alpha)$. Substituting the reflection formula yields $\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(x,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$. Hence these are the orthogonal root reflections of the chamber lemma. The roots span $V$, are reduced, and their reflection coefficients are integers, by the root datum. Its rational base $\Delta$ remains a real basis after scalar extension. Real proportionality of two rational roots implies rational proportionality by comparing a nonzero rational coordinate, so reducedness also holds over $\mathbf R$. Extending a rational linear map to this real basis preserves its matrix, so the faithful quotient action remains faithful on $V$.

source.place: C.19--C.20, p.611; finite averaging and the displayed reflection computation.

proof.text: The pairing identity gives $(\rho,\alpha)=(\alpha,\alpha)/2>0$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity] to the preceding real root system: $C=C_\Delta$ is a chamber containing $\rho$. If $w\rho=\rho$, the chambers $wC$ and $C$ contain the same point, hence coincide as connected components. Simple transitivity makes the induced reflection-group element the identity; faithfulness in [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization] then gives $w=1$ in the normalizer quotient.

The base $-\Delta$ has chamber $-C$. By the chamber theorem and the identification of $W$, there is a unique $w_0\in W$ with $w_0C=-C$. For $x\in C$ and $\beta\in\Phi^+$, invariance gives $(w_0x,w_0\beta)=(x,\beta)>0$. The positive roots for $-C$ are $-\Phi^+$, so $w_0\Phi^+\subseteq-\Phi^+$ and equality follows from the finite equal cardinalities. Conversely, if $w\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$, then for $x\in C$ and $\gamma\in\Phi^+$ one has $w^{-1}\gamma\in-\Phi^+$ and $(wx,\gamma)=(x,w^{-1}\gamma)<0$. Thus $wC$ meets $-C$, so the two chambers coincide; uniqueness gives $w=w_0$. Finally $w_0(-C)=-w_0C=C$, so $w_0^2C=C$ and simple transitivity and faithfulness give $w_0^2=1$.

source.place: 21.41, p.436, and Definition 21.72, p.447; explicit positive-root/chamber comparison.

proof.text: Reindexing the half sum by $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$ gives $w_0\rho=-\rho$. If $w\rho=-\rho=w_0\rho$, then $(w_0^{-1}w)\rho=\rho$; the stabilizer calculation gives $w_0^{-1}w=1$, hence $w=w_0$. The converse is the displayed sum identity. All equalities are rational character-space equalities, so do not require a restriction on $\operatorname{char}F$. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, its span is zero, and the faithful identification with the empty reflection-generated group gives $W=\{1\}$, $\rho=0$ and $w_0=1$; the pairing assertion is vacuous.
